# **Stewardship of the Model City: A Deep Analysis of Lewis Downing and the Downing and Sons Legacy**

The intersection of history and commerce in Anniston, Alabama, is perhaps best defined by the red brick and weathered mortar of Gurnee Avenue. To walk this street is to traverse the timeline of a city once dubbed the "Model City" for its meticulous industrial planning and early adoption of modern technologies.1 At the heart of this district, standing at the corner of 11th Street and Gurnee, is Downing and Sons—a business that is as much an institution as it is a retail outlet. Its proprietor, Lewis Downing, occupies a unique position in the contemporary Anniston landscape, serving not only as the third-generation shepherd of his family’s commercial legacy but also as the Vice Mayor and Councilman for Ward 1\.3 His story is one of generational transition, where the values of mid-century retail meet the complexities of twenty-first-century municipal governance.

## **The Crucible of Gurnee Avenue: Origins of a Commercial Icon**

The narrative of Downing and Sons is inextricably linked to the post-war economic optimism of Northeast Alabama. Founded in 1963, the business began under circumstances that have since become part of the local entrepreneurial lore.3 Lewis Downing’s grandfather, seeking a gallon of paint for his wife, visited a Mary Carter Paint Supply Store that was then located across the street from the current establishment. In a moment of serendipity that would redefine the family’s future, the store’s owner offered to sell the entire business for $600.3 The purchase was finalized, and the foundation of a multi-generational legacy was laid in the heart of downtown Anniston.3

Initially operating as a Mary Carter Paint Supply franchise, the business was forced to adapt when the national chain faced bankruptcy in the late 1960s or early 1970s.3 This challenge served as a catalyst for diversification. While the store transitioned to an affiliation with True Value Paint and Hardware, the family recognized that a hardware-only model would not suffice in a changing Anniston.3 It was Lewis’s grandmother who provided the creative pivot that would distinguish the store from its competitors: she introduced sewing notions and fabrics.3 This integration of the rugged (hardware and garden supplies) with the refined (designer fabrics and upholstery) created a unique market niche that allowed the business to endure while other traditional retailers succumbed to the rise of big-box stores.

| Feature | Description of Downing and Sons | Significance in Local Context |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Year Founded** | 1963 3 | One of the oldest continuous family-owned retail businesses in downtown. |
| **Current Ownership** | Lewis Downing (since 2017\) 6 | Marks the third generation of Downing family leadership. |
| **Primary Industry** | Fabric, Home, and Garden 7 | Hybrid model serving both functional (garden) and aesthetic (interior) needs. |
| **Notable Specialization** | European designer upholstery fabrics 8 | Attracts regional clientele interested in high-end restoration. |
| **Location** | 1030 Gurnee Avenue 5 | Situated within the Downtown Anniston Historic District.9 |

The physical presence of the store at 1030 Gurnee Avenue is significant. It sits within a district characterized by neoclassical and commercial architecture dating back to the late nineteenth century.9 The area has survived urban renewal phases, including an era of aluminum facades in the 1950s that briefly obscured the historic brickwork.9 For Downing and Sons, the building is not just a storefront; it is an artifact of Anniston’s industrial peak and its subsequent transition into a service and specialty retail economy.

## **The Fabric of Commerce: Services and Evolution**

Under Lewis Downing’s leadership, which began in earnest when he assumed full ownership in 2017, the business has seen a remarkable expansion, reportedly doubling its growth.6 This success is attributed to a meticulously curated inventory that balances the practical demands of Northeast Alabama residents with high-end specialty products. The store is divided into distinct functional zones that reflect the family’s adaptive history.7

### **The Garden and Lawn Division**

The garden center is a cornerstone of the business, catering to a community that values both hobbyist gardening and sustainable small-scale farming. Unlike standard hardware stores, Downing and Sons emphasizes organic solutions, offering products like Black Kow and Happy Frog fertilizers, alongside a comprehensive selection of bulk and packaged seeds.7 This focus on organic inputs and traditional garden tools like wheelbarrows and grass seed reinforces the "general store" atmosphere that attracts residents seeking expertise over mere volume.7

### **The Textile and Interior Side**

The interior side of the business represents the legacy of Downing’s grandmother and remains a primary draw for the store. It specializes in drapery and upholstery fabrics, including high-performance outdoor materials and leather hides.7 A unique service offered is the custom-cutting of polyurethane foam forms, which serves the regional upholstery industry and local DIY enthusiasts alike.7 By sourcing high-quality European fabrics at discounted prices, the business has positioned itself as a regional destination for home restoration, a critical service in a city like Anniston that boasts a significant stock of historic homes.2

### **Texture and Tangibility**

For Lewis Downing, the business is as much about the sensory experience as it is about the transaction. He has described his daily routine as beginning with the physical act of setting out plants at a quarter of eight in the morning.3 The sensory memories of his childhood—the smell of organic fertilizers, the texture of heavy upholstery fabrics, and even the "ink smell" from the nearby *Anniston Star* print shop where his mother worked—are woven into his professional identity.3 This tactile connection to the business explains the store’s longevity; it is a place where customers come for "personalized assistance" and to "figure out what is going to work for their projects".3

## **The Architecture of a Family: Robert and Lewis Downing**

To understand Lewis Downing’s civic and business philosophy, one must look at the influence of his father, Robert Downing. The elder Downing served as a Calhoun County Commissioner for sixteen years, from 1994 to 2010\.3 His tenure was marked by a commitment to environmental stewardship and a vision for regional redevelopment that directly paved the way for Lewis’s current role on the City Council.

### **Robert Downing: The Environmental Commissioner**

Robert Downing was often referred to by his colleagues as the "resident tree hugger".11 This was not a pejorative term but a recognition of his forward-thinking advocacy for energy efficiency and land conservation. He spearheaded a campaign through the National Association of Counties (NACo) to encourage the EPA to write energy-saving programs specifically for courthouses, a move that saved Calhoun County approximately $50,000 annually.11 This legacy of "forward-thinking" and "unanimous support" for sustainable practices reflects a family culture that values efficiency and long-term planning over short-term political gains.11

| Robert Downing’s Major Initiatives | Impact on Calhoun County |
| :---- | :---- |
| **McClellan Joint Powers Authority (JPA)** | Instrumental in redeveloping Fort McClellan after its 1999 closure.12 |
| **Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Programs** | Created energy-efficiency benchmarks for municipal buildings.11 |
| **Mountain Longleaf Pine County Seal** | Led the 2008 initiative to create a county identity based on heritage.13 |
| **Coastal Wetland Revitalization** | Part of broader regional environmental recovery efforts.11 |

Robert Downing’s most critical contribution was his role as a founder of the McClellan Joint Powers Authority (JPA).12 When Fort McClellan was closed in 1999, the psychological and economic blow to Anniston was severe.12 Robert Downing advocated for a master-planned community that would be "lasting for future generations," emphasizing an inclusive and broad-based approach.12 This perspective—that a governing body has a responsibility to those who will inhabit the city fifty years from now—is a recurring theme in Lewis Downing’s own political rhetoric.3

### **The Symbolic Transition**

The swearing-in of Lewis Downing as the Ward 1 councilman in December 2024 was a moment of profound familial and civic symbolism. He took the oath of office with his hand on his grandmother Downing’s Bible, which dates back to the early 1920s.3 This same Bible was used by his father when he was elected to the Calhoun County Commission.3 Robert Downing’s presence at the ceremony, "beaming with pride," underscored the transition of the family’s civic mission from the county level to the municipal level.3

## **The Reluctant Politician: Lewis Downing’s Municipal Mandate**

Lewis Downing’s entry into formal politics was not a calculated career move but rather a commitment born of a "milestone birthday" and a desire to be an "asset and not a liability" to his hometown.3 A lifelong resident of Anniston, Downing grew up on 10th Street in a house that he and his wife, Katie, would eventually buy and use to raise their own first two children.3 His roots in Ward 1 are literal; he is a product of its schools, its churches, and its business district.3

### **The 2024 Appointment**

Downing was first introduced to the Anniston City Council not through an election but by appointment. In December 2024, he was chosen unanimously by the council to fill the vacancy left by Jay Jenkins, who had resigned in October.3 This appointment placed him in a critical position during a period of intense redistricting and infrastructure planning. His first official act—moving to adjourn the meeting after being sworn in—showed a pragmatic, no-nonsense approach to governance that has since become his trademark.3

### **The August 2025 Election Result**

The 2025 municipal election served as the ultimate validation of Downing’s role on the council. Running for a full term in Ward 1, Downing faced three challengers: Benjamin New, John Squires, and Brenton Tolson.3 The results were a landslide victory for the incumbent, reflecting a high level of community trust in his dual role as merchant and councilman.

This mandate allowed Downing to assume the title of Vice Mayor, a role in which he serves as a primary deputy to Mayor Ciara Smith-Roston.1 The synergy between the young mayor (the city's first African American female mayor and its youngest-ever mayor) and the seasoned business owner Downing (a third-generation white businessman) represents a modern, collaborative face for Anniston governance.4

## **The Geography of Governance: Ward 1 and the McClellan Frontier**

Ward 1 is a diverse and geographically significant section of Anniston. It includes the historic downtown core—the "heartbeat" of the city—and a substantial portion of the former Fort McClellan.16 For Downing, representing this ward requires balancing the micro-needs of downtown business owners with the macro-challenges of large-scale land redevelopment.

### **Downtown Revitalization and Infrastructure**

As the owner of a downtown business, Downing is uniquely attuned to the granular issues that impact urban quality of life. At a March 2026 town hall meeting, he addressed concerns ranging from jake brakes on the eastern bypass to litter and rodent control.3 His approach to infrastructure is data-driven; he has advocated for a ![][image9] million to ![][image10] million paving plan that uses municipal consultants to prioritize roads based on traffic volume and resident density rather than political favoritism.3

His leadership in Main Street Anniston and the Anniston Downtown Development Authority has provided him with a toolkit for urban renewal.6 He view the revitalization of downtown not just as an economic goal, but as a moral one—preserving the history of the "Model City" while making it viable for modern commerce. This is evidenced by his support for initiatives like the ![][image11] pitch competition for local entrepreneurs, which aims to diversify the business offerings on Noble and Gurnee Streets.18

### **The McClellan Vision**

Development at McClellan is perhaps the most significant challenge facing the current council. Downing has emphasized "honest, responsible leadership" in managing the 18,000-acre site.3 His focus is on projects that expand the city’s tax base, such as attracting large-scale commercial developments and potentially high-end residential projects.3 However, he has also urged caution regarding "young" industries like AI data centers, expressing concern over their long-term impact on local resources and community stability.3

The redevelopment of the former Starships property into a studio project at McClellan is one example of the creative repurposing Downing supports.3 This aligns with his father’s earlier vision of making McClellan a hub for the arts, which once included the Alabama Symphony’s summer home in the historic warehouse district.12 For Lewis Downing, McClellan is the "extraordinary asset" that can ensure Anniston’s prosperity well into the future.3

## **The Merchant as Citizen: Texture of a Local Legend**

To categorize Lewis Downing solely by his business or his political seat is to miss the "texture" that defines his role in Anniston. He is a man who values the simplicity of a "good companion" (his dog Greta) and the resonance of rock and roll and bluegrass music.3 His favorite film, *The Last of the Mohicans*, hints at a person who appreciates narratives of duty and the weight of history.3

### **Civic Leadership and "Asset" Mentality**

Downing’s involvement in community organizations is extensive and reflects a holistic approach to city improvement. He doesn't just sit on boards; he leads them.

* **Main Street Anniston:** As Chairman, he led the efforts to bring people back to the downtown core.6  
* **Spirit of Anniston:** Served as a Board Member focused on strengthening civic bonds.6  
* **West Anniston Community Development:** Focused on quality-of-life improvements for residents in historically neglected areas.6  
* **Downtown Development Authority:** Contributed to economic development strategies that helped businesses like his own double their growth.6

This "asset" mentality—the idea that one must do their part to be a benefit to the city—is a core tenant of his biography. He admits to never finishing his degree at the University of Alabama or Jacksonville State University because he was pulled back by the gravity of the family business.3 This lack of a formal credential in his early years has not hindered his professional success; rather, it has made him a champion for practical experience and hands-on leadership.6

### **The Gurnee Avenue Context: 1030 vs. 1031**

The location of Downing and Sons at 1030 Gurnee Avenue places it directly across an alley from 1031 Gurnee Avenue—the site of the former Greyhound Bus Depot and now the Freedom Riders National Monument.20 This proximity is laden with historical significance. The alley between the two buildings was where a bus carrying Freedom Riders was attacked by a mob on May 14, 1961\.20

Downing’s business operates in the shadow of this site of national historical trauma and triumph. His support for the downtown historic district—including the designation of the Mural Building and the expansion of the National Register boundaries—demonstrates an understanding that Anniston’s future is built on an honest accounting of its past.20 The "Model City" legacy is complicated, and Downing’s role as a business owner and city leader requires navigating the tension between preserving nineteenth-century architecture and memorializing twentieth-century civil rights struggles.

## **Conclusion: Stewardship in the Post-Industrial Era**

The profile of Lewis Downing that emerges from the archives of *The Anniston Star* and the official records of the City of Anniston is one of a "merchant-statesman".4 He is a man who understands that the health of a city is measured by more than just its municipal bonds; it is measured by the vibrancy of its sidewalks and the success of the neighbors who live in its wards.

Downing and Sons remains a "cornerstone" of the community not because it is a relic, but because it is a living example of adaptation.6 By combining high-performance European fabrics with organic fertilizers and "painfully honest" customer service, the business provides a template for the kind of "responsible development" Downing advocates for on the council.3

As Vice Mayor, Downing represents the "heartbeat" of downtown Anniston.3 His leadership on the City Council, informed by three generations of business experience and a father’s legacy of environmentalism, offers a steady hand for a city navigating the transition from a "soil pipe" manufacturing hub to a diversified, modern community.1 In the narrative of Northeast Alabama, Lewis Downing stands as a "Southern Legend" of a practical sort: one who believes that the best way to honor the history of a city is to work hard every day to ensure it has a future.
